title: Things to do in Bologna: 5 places, porticoes and San Luca
description: Explore five places in Bologna with a city-centre walking route, Archiginnasio booking advice and practical choices for reaching San Luca.
relatedQueries: Bologna walking route and San Luca
intro: For a first visit to Bologna, combine Piazza Maggiore, San Petronio, the Archiginnasio, Santo Stefano and the Sanctuary of San Luca. The first four belong to a city-centre walk; the fifth requires a separate trip towards the hills. Understanding that distinction is more useful than squeezing five names into the hours before your train.

The route moves between a civic square, religious buildings, a former university seat and a long porticoed approach. This guide explains what to look for and which decisions matter at each stop. There is a flexible full-day outline and a slower option with an overnight stay. Official information was checked on 7 November 2026; the documentary photographs are archive images.

sections.heading: 1. Piazza Maggiore: understand the centre before entering buildings
paragraphs: Piazza Maggiore provides a useful point of orientation. San Petronio, Palazzo d’Accursio, Palazzo del Podestà, Palazzo dei Notai and Palazzo dei Banchi surround it. The tourism office describes a square shaped through successive changes and associated with municipal life and trade. Looking at the ensemble helps explain why Bologna is more than one memorable façade.

Begin at an edge, then notice how the perspective changes as you move towards the middle. Compare the civic buildings with the basilica and decide which interior interests you most. Enjoying the public square does not require an attraction ticket; entering a palace, tower or collection is a separate experience with its own conditions.

This is a useful first stop if you arrive without an immediate booking. It can also serve as a meeting point or somewhere to reconsider your route in wet weather. Porticoes provide shelter on many city streets, but the entire walk is not indoors. Allow time for crossings, pauses and any temporary installations in the squares.

sections.heading: 2. San Petronio: an unfinished façade and different visitor experiences
paragraphs: The Basilica of San Petronio occupies one side of Piazza Maggiore. Construction began in 1390, and its façade was only partly clad in marble. The contrast between the lower section and the brickwork above is worth examining before going inside. Three naves and their side chapels give the interior a very different scale from the square.

Choose a few details rather than trying to examine every feature at once. Cassini’s meridian line and the chapels shift the focus from urban space to scientific instruments, painting and architecture. The basilica remains a place of worship, so sightseeing must fit around services and instructions from staff.

Check the exact experience you are booking. Bologna Welcome identifies certain chapels, including the Bolognini or Three Kings Chapel, as requiring a separate ticket. General access should not be treated as access to every possible visit, and a purchase for a different attraction does not automatically cover this one. Verify the rooms included if a particular work is the main reason for coming.

sections.heading: 3. Archiginnasio: a university courtyard and the Anatomical Theatre
paragraphs: The Archiginnasio makes university history tangible. Built in 1562–1563, it served as the University’s seat until 1803. Its porticoed courtyard and heraldic decoration reward a pause before you even consider visiting the rooms upstairs. Look at the relationship between the open courtyard, vaulted passages and decorated walls instead of treating it only as a queueing area.

The practical distinction is important: entering the building is not the same as visiting the Anatomical Theatre or Stabat Mater Hall. Official visitor information requires booked tickets for these experiences and notes that institutional activities can make some rooms unavailable. The library serves readers and researchers; it is not a freely accessible tourist attraction.

Secure the time of any booked visit before arranging the rest of the walk. The principal entrance is on Piazza Galvani, while the tourism office identifies a separate lift entrance on via de’ Foscherari for visitors with reduced mobility. Check current instructions before travelling. The photograph here shows the courtyard, rather than the Anatomical Theatre or a promise that every room will be open.

sections.heading: 4. Santo Stefano: give the square time
paragraphs: Piazza Santo Stefano opens from the street of the same name towards the religious complex traditionally called the Seven Churches. The space lets you appreciate both the complex’s frontage and the palaces along its sides. Its interest lies in the relationship between buildings, entrances and public space, rather than a visit organised around a single object.

Approach along the street, then view the square from the opposite end. A small change in position helps reveal its shape and a sensible place to pause without blocking an entrance. If you want to enter the complex, check its conditions separately. The traditional Seven Churches name does not guarantee seven rooms or churches open at the same time.

This stop balances a morning spent indoors. It does not need another reservation to earn its place in the route. If time is short, choose between lingering here and rushing away towards San Luca. Time spent observing materials, façades and everyday movement often adds more than another hurried transfer.

sections.heading: 5. San Luca: protect a separate block for the hillside
paragraphs: The Sanctuary of San Luca stands on Colle della Guardia. According to Bologna Welcome, its porticoed connection from Porta Saragozza extends for around four kilometres and has more than six hundred arches. It forms part of Bologna’s portico heritage inscribed by UNESCO in 2021. Distance and climbing make this a distinct outing rather than another flat city-centre stop.

If you plan to walk, consider the return as well as the climb and choose an effort level that suits you. The portico does not remove the gradient or guarantee comfortable temperatures throughout the journey. If you prefer transport, check the actual service and departure point for your date; this guide does not assume a transfer is included in a general tourist pass.

Distinguish the sanctuary visit from the panoramic terrace. Services can restrict sightseeing, and official information separates basilica access from the dome and crypt. Access arrangements are not identical for every area. Choose San Luca for the route and setting, then treat any additional climb to a viewpoint as a separate decision.

sections.heading: Order the walk around your own priorities
paragraphs: If the Archiginnasio is essential, start with its reservation. Group Piazza Maggiore and San Petronio around that visit, then continue towards Santo Stefano. This reduces backtracking without assigning the same duration to every attraction. Someone interested in painting may spend far longer inside a chapel than a traveller focused on exterior architecture.

Keep an independent block for San Luca and avoid completing the climb against a tightly timed train departure. With an overnight stay, you can explore the centre first and visit the sanctuary the next morning. If you only have a few hours, enjoying the four central places and saving the hill for another trip is a coherent alternative.

sections.heading: Tickets, mobility and a budget that matches the trip
paragraphs: Separate transport, meals and individual visits when planning your budget. A public square, building access and a reserved visitor room are different experiences. Before comparing a tourist card with individual tickets, list the spaces you actually want, their opening dates and what each option includes. This selection does not assume automatic savings or offer one price for every traveller.

For a trip involving reduced mobility, plan each building entrance and the sanctuary transfer individually. The documented Archiginnasio lift does not describe gradients elsewhere in the city. Wear suitable walking shoes in any season and leave a proper meal break. Religious services and institutional use can alter a visit even when the outdoor square remains accessible.

itinerary: City-centre morning: start in Piazza Maggiore, examine the palaces and enter San Petronio if services and your interests allow. Continue to the Archiginnasio courtyard and keep the booked time for its visitor rooms; the courtyard is not a substitute for that ticket.

Next section: walk towards Santo Stefano and give the square an unhurried pause. Decide whether your energy and remaining time support a hillside outing. Completing all five places at any cost is not necessary for a rewarding first visit.

San Luca or a second morning: allow a dedicated block for the sanctuary, with the outward and return journeys arranged. Staying overnight lets you separate the portico walk from the central route and removes the pressure of a last-minute rush.

faq.question: Can I visit these five places in one day?
faq.answer: You can combine them with selective interior visits and a separate plan for San Luca. With limited time, concentrating on the centre is more sensible than adding a hurried hillside trip.

faq.question: Can tourists visit the Archiginnasio library like a museum?
faq.answer: No. Official information identifies the library as a study space. Tourist visits concern specific areas, including the Anatomical Theatre and Stabat Mater Hall, with booking and availability conditions.

faq.question: Does general San Petronio access include every chapel?
faq.answer: Do not assume so: certain chapels require a separate ticket. Check the specific space you want and the conditions published for the date of your visit.

faq.question: Is the walk to San Luca flat?
faq.answer: No. The sanctuary is on a hill, and the porticoed route from Porta Saragozza adds distance and climbing. Choose the approach according to your mobility and include the return journey in your plan.

conclusion: Bologna comes into focus through its civic centre, religious buildings, university spaces and hillside. Choose paid visits for a reason and let squares and porticoes connect the route. A balanced day is more useful than completing the list without time to look.
